item.title: 'Scream' star admits he's 'ashamed' of sequel return after actress fired over anti-Israel comments
item.description: Matthew Lillard says he feels "ashamed" for returning to "Scream 7" after Melissa Barrera's firing, calling himself on the "wrong side of history."
item.content:encoded:
"Scream" actor Matthew Lillard said Tuesday that he felt "ashamed" for returning to the horror franchise after actress Melissa Barrera was fired over social media posts about Israel and the war in Gaza, telling fans during a 30th anniversary screening in Austin, Texas, that he believed he ended up on the "wrong side of history."

Lillard, who reprised his role as Stu Macher in the seventh installment, said his excitement about returning to the franchise overshadowed his concerns about how Barrera had been treated.

As reported by Entertainment Weekly, Lillard said, "I went back to do Scream, and I got called out. And I’m like, ‘Oh, f---. That’s brutal.’" "I feel bad about that. I feel ashamed about that. Because in that moment I was so excited to go back, I didn’t really think about Melissa and that journey."

"I’m embarrassed, that’s the truth… I blew that. I’m on the wrong side of history for that. I still like being in the movie [but] it may not have been the best idea," Lillard continued.

PEREZ HILTON JOINS 'TOMI LAHREN IS FEARLESS' AND DECLARES CANCEL CULTURE IS NOW A SPORT

Barrera was dropped from the franchise in November 2023 after publishing and sharing a series of posts criticizing Israel following Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack.

In one post previously reported by Fox News Digital, Barrera accused Israel of committing "genocide" and "ethnic cleansing" in Gaza.

"Gaza is currently being treated like a concentration camp," Barrera said. "Cornering everyone together, with no where to go, no electricity no water … People have [learned] nothing from our histories. And just like our histories, people are still silently watching it all happen. THIS IS GENOCIDE & ETHNIC CLEANSING."

In another post, Barrera claimed Western news outlets were disproportionately presenting Israel's side of the conflict and told followers to draw their own conclusions about why.

‘NO JEWS, NO NEWS’ STRIKES AGAIN AS SELECTIVE COVERAGE OF THE 'UNSETTLERS' FUELS ANTI-ISRAEL ANGER

"Because western media only shows the other side. Why they do that, I will let you deduce for yourself," Barrera said.

Spyglass denied at the time that Barrera was removed merely for supporting Palestinians, instead saying it viewed some of her rhetoric as antisemitic.

"Spyglass’ stance is unequivocally clear: We have zero tolerance for antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form, including false references to genocide, ethnic cleansing, Holocaust distortion or anything that flagrantly crosses the line into hate speech," the company said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Spyglass Media for comment about Lillard's remarks. 

Barrera subsequently rejected the suggestion that she was promoting antisemitism and defended her criticism of governments, Fox News Digital reported in May.

MORE THAN 180 JEWISH ENTERTAINERS RALLY BEHIND ACTOR MARK RUFFALO IN PROTEST LETTER

"I believe a group of people are not their leadership and that no governing body should be above criticism. I pray day and night for no more deaths, for no more violence and for peaceful co-existence," Barrera said.

The controversy resurfaced earlier this year when Barrera criticized former cast-mates who returned to the franchise without her. When asked whether actors who went back for "Scream 7" were "scabby," Barrera agreed.

"One hundred percent. I think they all are," Barrera said. "And they have to live with that."

At Tuesday’s screening, Lillard directly defended Barrera’s position and criticized the lack of public support she received after her firing.

"Melissa Barrera, who’s a beautiful actor, was fired for what she said after the whole Palestinian... what started happening in Israel," Lillard said. "It’s really f-—– bulls--- and really hard, and she’s on the right side of history."

"When that happened to Melissa, the whole world didn’t pipe up, but she was a year early on what the f---’s going on. But the whole world should have popped up and said, ‘She’s right.’ And they didn’t. And that’s brutal."

Despite the upheaval surrounding its development, "Scream 7" was released Feb. 27 and eventually crossed $200 million at the global box office, becoming the highest-grossing film in the franchise’s history, according to Paramount. The film shifted its focus back to Neve Campbell’s Sidney Prescott and brought back several franchise veterans, including Lillard.

When reached for comment by Fox News Digital, Hollywood in Toto editor Christian Toto said of Lillard’s remarks: "Now that the Palestinian cause is spiking in his far-Left industry, he has regrets. Now. Months after shooting the film. Months after its release. Months after the actress in question lost the role." 

Toto added, "Will he give all the money back? Does he know what she actually said about Israel and the timing of those comments? Is he aware of other artists who have had their free speech rights trampled?"

item.title: Roger Goodell details NFL expansion possibilities and a timetable for a full season of international games
item.description: Roger Goodell says Europe is the most likely home for NFL international expansion, envisioning two new franchise teams outside the United States.
item.content:encoded:
Commissioner Roger Goodell made the rounds during the NFL's first week of the regular season and into Thursday night's opening of the new Highmark Stadium in Buffalo. Out of that travel that spanned continents, we're getting a picture of his plans for league expansion.

Bottom line: Goodell sees NFL expansion outside the United States on the horizon.

"I think if we continue to grow, continue to get the kind of reaction, I do think a franchise will be international at some point in time," Goodell said prior to the Thursday night game between the Buffalo Bills and Detroit Lions on Prime's pregame show.

"I think Europe is the most likely [place], for a lot of reasons. One, the length of time we've been playing there. But also, the scheduling is going to be a lot easier."

ROGER GOODELL DISMISSES 49ERS COACH'S CONCERNS ABOUT PLAYING IN AUSTRALIA, SAYS IT'S PART OF LONG-TERM PLAN

The NFL began playing regular-season games in Europe in 2007 and to date has played 55 regular-season games there.

One could also argue Europe makes sense for international expansion because most of the teams in the AFC East and NFC East and some teams in the AFC South and NFC South are within a seven-hour flight to, say, London.

Other places simply don't make similar sense at this time.

"Australia might create a few complications for us," Goodell admitted.

NFL TO COMMEMORATE 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 TERRORIST ATTACKS ACROSS ALL ITS STADIUMS AND EVEN IN AUSTRALIA

Goodell apparently is not thinking about expanding by one team in Europe. That would throw off the league's 32-team symmetry.

"I also believe we could have more than one team, which I think, ultimately, the support is there," Goodell said. "Two more teams."

So when will all this happen?

Goodell recently signed a new contract that carries his tenure as commissioner through the 2030 season. There has been speculation his goal is to have international expansion by the time his contract expires.

Is that the timeline?

"I don't think so," Goodell said on the Netflix pregame show recently. "There was no connection to the two.

"You know, listen, our vision here is to make it a global sport. The NFL deserves to be, it's a great game, and we all believe in it passionately."

But while expansion by the end of the contract isn't a Goodell goal, having a full season's worth of international games is definitely on his radar.

This year the NFL is playing nine games abroad. Next year that number rises to a record 10 international games.

"I think our work here will be to get to 16 regular-season [International] games," Goodell said. "When we get to that point, then we'll be looking for the next, you know, stage to grow. But we think we'll be there in a few years.

"That may happen within four years."

item.title: GOP lawmakers smell something else behind Big Tech's AI doomsday warnings: 'Something else going on'
item.description: Capitol Hill lawmakers question whether OpenAI and Anthropic are pushing for AI regulation to stifle competition and lock in market dominance.
item.content:encoded:
Republicans on Capitol Hill are grappling over whether and how to regulate artificial intelligence companies even as top AI business leaders warn the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.

The simmering debate over AI guardrails has exploded this week as House lawmakers worked through their final week in Washington until after the midterm elections. The flurry of activity was partially spurred by tech CEOs like Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman warning that the pace of innovation should be slowed after both companies saw AI models hack into other organizations of their own accord.

And while some in Congress are demanding swift action, others who spoke with Fox News Digital are questioning the motivation of AI companies in calling for the government to step in.

"I think there's a false sense of urgency," Rep. Troy Downing, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital.

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL

Downing spent his young adulthood in tech, having previously been a research scientist at the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences at New York University and founding online calendar company WebCal, which was later acquired by Yahoo!.

"Yes, we should be taking it seriously, but I think the hyperbole is misplaced right now," Downing said. "Any one of those people crying gloom and doom has the possibility of stopping it in their own shops, so there's something else going on there."

Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C., a former assistant U.S. attorney, also doubted AI companies' motives.

AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK

"I'm very skeptical of people in big business who want to leverage big government to suppress competition," Knott said. "I'm afraid that's what we're seeing. That'd be like ... Google, Yahoo, Microsoft, Apple saying, 'We need to regulate all tech.' Whether it's software or hardware. It's like, guys, you're here already, right? And if there's one thing that I'm confident in, to protect AI for good, there has to be more than one option."

Still others believe lawmakers do not broadly have enough knowledge to take on AI guardrails.

Rep. Jimmy Patronis, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital that Congress should instead repeal Section 230, a federal law shielding internet and tech companies from liability for what third parties post.

"I think the warning is real, and I think that AI is unbelievable — look, AI is going to cure cancer. AI is going to find solutions to get rid of diseases that we never thought we could get rid of, but it does need to have some oversight. It needs a kill switch," Patronis conceded. "But again, I don't think Congress has the expertise to tell an emerging technology what's the best way to go."

Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., said when asked if Congress should act before the end of this year, "It's too complex a subject. You've got to understand it."

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump also joined the debate by dismissing AI companies' calls for more government regulation.

TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’

"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," he wrote on Truth Social. "The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!"

But others are pushing for the government to step in to at least some degree, with some Republicans arguing for human guardrails to ensure AI does not go too far by itself.

RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS

"The sooner we can act, the better," Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., chair of the House's AI task force, told reporters Wednesday. "Certainly, we've had some warning shots lately that have been very concerning ... So, God forbid we have a Chernobyl moment at some point here that really causes harm to people and focuses the public's attention on AI in a way that we hope it will never be."

When asked by Fox News Digital about Trump's warning, however, he said, "I think the president was talking about the dangers of over-regulation, and that's something I very much agree with him on."

RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION

Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., held a press conference alongside Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., on Thursday pushing legislation to stop "rogue" AI agents such as those that broke out of containment during trials by OpenAI and Anthropic.

"We want to make sure that people remain in control. This isn't about stopping AI or stifling innovation," Lawler said. "Some states have put a moratorium on the infrastructure that powers this technology. That does not invent a kill switch."

Gottheimer said the bill "tells the National Institute of Standards and Technology [to] get in a room and set standards, so organizations can find every agent on their network, verify who built it, who's running it, watch it in real time for anything suspicious, and cut off its access the second something looks wrong."

item.title: Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton tells Macklemore he is ‘standing’ in solidarity with him on Palestine
item.description: Lewis Hamilton pledged to stand in solidarity with Macklemore after his "Free Palestine" messaging got him removed from Ed Sheeran's "Loop Tour."
item.content:encoded:
Pop star Macklemore has generated quite a buzz recently with his "Free Palestine" messaging while on Ed Sheeran's "Loop Tour."

The 43-year-old musician was kicked off the tour following backlash from his pro-Palestine stance, but there have been a few "woke" celebrities who have come to Macklemore's defense.

Following the Seattle native's pledge to donate $1 million to Palestinian aid organizations, children's YouTube star Ms. Rachel said she would match his donation and urged "every wealthy White celebrity" to do the same.

MACKLEMORE DONATES $1M TO PALESTINIAN AID ORGANIZATIONS AFTER ED SHEERAN TOUR FALLOUT

Ms. Rachel isn't the only one to throw her public support behind Macklemore, though, as Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton took to social media to praise the rapper for his stance.

Hamilton commented under Macklemore's Instagram statement on the matter, pledging to "stand" in solidarity with him.

COLIN KAEPERNICK ACCUSES NFL OF 'COLLUDING' AGAINST MACKLEMORE AMID 'FREE PALESTINE' CONTROVERSY

If you know anything about Hamilton, then this shouldn't come as a shock.

The 41-year-old was at the forefront of the Black Lives Matter movement, especially when it reached a fever pitch following the death of George Floyd in 2020.

Hamilton took part in the protesting of the U.S. National Anthem, kneeling during its playing before every Grand Prix event he entered in that same year.

He's been spotted wearing shirts supporting causes linked to Black Lives Matter quite often and has also been a vocal supporter of LGBTQ+ issues.

Between those incidents and his past comments about Formula One's lack of diversity - Hamilton is mixed-race and is the only Black driver in the sport - it's easy to see why he was so quick to jump on the bandwagon to support Macklemore for his pro-Palestine stance.

As others continue to excoriate the rapper for his "Free Palestine" messaging, such as Barstool founder Dave Portnoy, you can expect many more on the other side of the aisle to voice their support for him.

It's an issue that has been around for a long time, and it certainly isn't going away any time soon.

item.title: Duncan Sheik, ‘Barely Breathing’ singer, dead at 56
item.description: Duncan Sheik, the voice behind "Barely Breathing" and Tony-winning "Spring Awakening," died from organ failure at 56, his mother confirmed.
item.content:encoded:
Duncan Sheik, the singer-songwriter behind the hit "Barely Breathing" and the Tony and Grammy-winning musical "Spring Awakening," has died. He was 56.

Sheik died Thursday from organ failure, his mother, Suzanne Sheik, told The New York Times. 

Representatives for Sheik did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

While "Barely Breathing" made Sheik a familiar voice on ’90s radio, Broadway ultimately became a defining chapter of his career.

"With the exception of our director, we are all kind of Broadway outsiders. We wanted to shake things up a bit. And we just set out to make this really cool piece of theater," Sheik told The Associated Press in 2007 of "Spring Awakening."

Sheik is survived by his wife, Nora Ariffin, and their 7-year-old daughter, Ines.

This is a breaking news story. Please check back for more developments.

item.title: Pilot’s sudden death during overnight layover puts spotlight on fatigue concerns
item.description: An Air India captain, Sunny Sharad Asaldekar, 46, was found unresponsive in his New Delhi hotel room during a layover, sparking renewed fatigue concerns for pilots.
item.content:encoded:
An Air India captain was found unresponsive in his hotel room during an overnight flight layover in New Delhi, and was later pronounced dead at a hospital.

The captain has been identified as Sunny Sharad Asaldekar, 46, The New Indian Express reported. He had checked into the hotel on Thursday, and his brother contacted the hotel manager the following evening after Asaldekar stopped answering calls.

The hotel manager entered the locked room with a master key and found Asaldekar unconscious and unresponsive, according to the outlet.

'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS

Police responded to the hotel, and Asaldekar was taken to a hospital, where he was declared dead.

"Air India is deeply saddened at the passing away of a cockpit crew member in Delhi last night," the airline said in a statement to The New Indian Express.

"He was on a layover rest at a hotel in Delhi where he was found unconscious last evening. He was rushed to the hospital immediately, where he was declared dead."

A post-mortem examination was conducted, but the cause of death has not yet been determined.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The Federation of Indian Pilots renewed its call for an urgent review of fatigue-management practices after the pilot's death but said it was not directly linking fatigue to his death, according to The Times of India.

Matthew "Whiz" Buckley, a former U.S. Navy F/A-18 Hornet fighter pilot who also flew for American Airlines and FedEx, told Fox News Digital that fatigue has long been a concern in commercial aviation.

"Pilot fatigue in aviation has been an issue since day one," Buckley said.

While passengers may assume an overnight layover gives pilots plenty of time to recover, Buckley said required rest does not always mean pilots get enough sleep.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

"A layover is just that. It's a crew laying over in a city that is not their home base," he said.

Pilots may arrive at a hotel in the early morning hours and then try to sleep during the day, Buckley said, which can work against the body's natural sleep cycle.

"It's just unnatural to sleep during off hours," he said.

Buckley said he faced that challenge while flying overnight routes himself — and that pilot fatigue was among the reasons he made changes in his career.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Long-haul flights can be especially difficult when pilots cross multiple time zones, he added.

"Where it really takes a toll on the body for pilots is east-west," Buckley said. "When you're crossing multiple time zones, [that's] when your body can really get messed up."

Fatigue can also build up beyond one flight or layover, according to Buckley, who cited irregular hours and prolonged periods of sitting, plus diet issues, exercise challenges and time away from family as factors that can affect pilots.

Buckley said U.S. safeguards include federal crew-rest requirements, airline policies and labor agreements, but pilots also play a key role in deciding whether they are fit to fly.

"At the end of the day ... you know who determines if a pilot is fit to fly? You," Buckley said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Air India for comment.

item.title: Young swing-state voters cozy up to Democratic Socialists, say party establishment must ‘learn’ from DSA wins
item.description: Young Michigan voters at Abdul El-Sayed's rally explain why Democratic Socialists of America's platform on Medicare for All appeals to them.
item.content:encoded:
Gen Z and young Millennial voters in Michigan who are leaning blue for the midterm election say they welcome the ideas of the Democratic Socialists of America, with a couple of voters agreeing that Americans should abolish the Senate.

Fox News Digital was on the ground at Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's "Students v. Billionaires" rally at Michigan State University on Sept. 11 and at the Detroit Health Department's annual block party, where young Democratic voters said rising costs and the complacency of the Democratic establishment have made the DSA more appealing to them.

"I feel as if they actually focus on the people," said Detroit resident Shelby Campbell, who is also a 2023 Wayne State University graduate. "It's not as, I guess, capitalistic or just bought into the system. They want to do good, but they are just another big organization, and I think we just need to get rid of all the political parties and be independent."

SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES'

So far this election cycle, dozens of Democratic Socialists of America candidates have won their primary races, including Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney, who defeated incumbent Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich.

But some of the biggest upsets came out of New York, where New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democratic Socialists of America member, saw three candidates he endorsed — Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Brad Lander — win their Democratic congressional primaries.

The flurry of DSA-backed primary victories has put Republicans on the offensive while fueling concern among some Democrats about the socialist movement’s growing influence within the party.

Noel Otteson is a sophomore at Michigan State University. He described himself as a "leftist" and "anti-capitalist," but he said he supports El-Sayed for his Medicare for All stance and his promise to get money out of politics.

SCHUMER DODGES QUESTION ON WHETHER DSA BELONGS IN DEMOCRATIC PARTY

"I believe in the power of people and democracy over corporations and oligarchs running everything, putting millions upon millions if not billions of dollars into Congress too," Otteson told Fox News Digital.

"The system is rigged against the average person and is in favor of corporations and special interests and lobbyists," Otteson continued.

Otteson said he supports the DSA's proposal to abolish the U.S. Senate, which he called "undemocratic."

"The way that the Senate is set up is inherently undemocratic," Otteson said. "I'm someone who always, always, prioritizes democracy, and the Senate isn't that."

"Some states hold more power than others based on population, and I would probably advocate for a more parliamentary system, you know, things like the U.K. and a lot of other European countries have, or most other countries have actually," Otteson said.

NEWSOM ADMITS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST IDEAS ‘MAINSTREAM’ IN DEMOCRAT PARTY: ‘PRETTY ALIGNED’

He proposed that the House of Representatives should be expanded.

And in the heart of Detroit, Jahdante Smith, who is a Green Party candidate for District 9 of the Michigan House of Representatives, agreed that the Senate has got to go.

"Their stance on abolishing the Senate, I think that is something that can work, only because the Senate is one of the most exclusionary clubs in politics and is also very, very hard to get into, and I think if you have a Republican and Democrat in the U.S. Senate in one state, they kind of cancel each other out, and they really don't get anything positive done," Smith told Fox News Digital.

Smith said he supports the DSA's anti-ICE agenda and Medicare for All proposals, but wants to see the organization bring about actual change.

"I support their ideas, but I love to see them have more traction in getting things actually done. Policy is something that you have to enact. It's not bills die in Congress, bills die on Capitol Hill every day," Smith told Fox News Digital. "You have to be able to get those bills passed through. I do support their stance on anti-ice."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Blake, a Michigan State University freshman, said he likes a lot of what the Democratic Socialists of America is pushing but said he's not on board with everything on its agenda, including abolishing the Senate.

"The standard democrat has shown themselves to more or less be incapable of standing up for themselves and standing up for what's right," Blake told Fox News Digital. "So I've leaned on, I've decided to take my allegiances with further parties on more extreme sides of leftism because they can do what needs to be done."

"And I feel like that's a lesson that normal Democrats need to learn," Blake continued.

item.title: Reaction to ‘Ted Lasso’ shows left-wing critics are never satisfied, so why does Hollywood keep trying?
item.description: 'Ted Lasso' Season 4 built its entire plot around women's soccer and feminist themes, yet progressive critics still said the show failed women.
item.content:encoded:
Apple’s major hit show "Ted Lasso" centered its return on women’s soccer and nearly every grievance progressive critics prioritize. They still said it failed women.

It should serve as a reminder to Hollywood that trying to please people who are never satisfied is a losing battle. And Hollywood really should stop ruining good shows trying to chase that approval.

Now, I loved the first two seasons of "Ted Lasso." The third season wasn't as good, but I watched the entire thing.

So, when Apple brought the show back after a three-year hiatus, I was willing to give Season 4 a chance.

I didn't make it through the premiere.

During the opening sequence, Ted is working at a Kansas City grocery store and casually stealing food from his employer. When a coworker asks whether he worries about getting caught, Ted says he doesn't, "probably due to my deeply ingrained white male privilege."

It was a throwaway joke that arrived almost immediately, before the show established its new story or gave viewers much of a reason to care. It felt deliberate, like the writers were telling the audience exactly what kind of season this would be.

RIDICULOUS USA TODAY COLUMN PROVES THAT THE DEMAND FOR MISOGYNY IN SPORTS FAR EXCEEDS THE SUPPLY

Then came the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum scene.

Leslie Higgins visits the museum after discovering that the American Jazz Museum is closed for a private event. A tour guide explains how Black baseball players, including Satchel Paige, were denied opportunities in Major League Baseball because of segregation.

Higgins responds by comparing their experience to women once being prohibited from playing soccer in England.

Using the color barrier in American baseball as a narrative bridge to the challenges facing a fictional English women's soccer team felt painfully forced and over-the-top.

My wife rolled her eyes. I looked at her and asked whether there was any reason to keep watching.

She agreed there wasn't.

So, we turned it off.

I couldn't stomach watching the remaining episodes, but I did review the transcripts of all seven that Apple has released as of Sept. 17. I paid particularly close attention to the first four episodes, which were among those provided to television critics before the season premiered.

Those transcripts confirmed exactly what the opening episode suggested: Gender politics aren't a minor component of the new season.

They are the season.

The second episode revolves heavily around whether Rebecca is sufficiently feminist after hiring Ted to coach AFC Richmond's new women's team.

Alice Chilton, who helped construct the team, tells Rebecca she is resigning after being passed over for the head-coaching position. Before leaving, Alice asks Rebecca whether she considered her for the job.

Rebecca says no.

Alice then asks whether Rebecca considered any woman.

Again, Rebecca says no.

This sends Rebecca into a panic over whether she is supportive enough of women. She begins reading feminist literature and delivers a painfully awkward press-conference speech declaring that women are "just as capable and compelling as men" and that "the future is female."

She then introduces the manager of Richmond's women's team, "who just happens to be a man."

The show plays Rebecca's desperation for laughs. But the underlying conflict is whether Ted, as a man, should have received the opportunity at all.

Remember what Ted accomplished with Richmond. He took the club through relegation, earned promotion back to the Premier League and then led it to second place after entering the final day of the season with a chance to win the championship.

Ted was overqualified to coach a brand-new second-division women's team. Yet the show treats Rebecca's decision to hire him as evidence that she might have failed women.

The first four episodes introduce several predictable progressive talking points surrounding supposed oppression of women in sports: lower salaries, inferior facilities, inadequate media coverage and a lack of financial support. One might argue that those are products of capitalism and not some nefarious plot to hold down female athletes, but I digress.

Then comes a cascade of storylines centered on female athletes, as if the writers had a checklist and had to make sure they hit them all. One player leaves the team after becoming pregnant. A single mother brings her child to open tryouts because she couldn't arrange childcare. Sponsors threaten to abandon the team, while male shareholders mock the entire idea as a waste of money.

Then Zelda Southport, a wealthy investor in women's sports, delivers a speech accusing executives of using women's soccer for "reputation-laundering" while hiding their "fake allyship." She invokes the "patriarchy" for good measure.

Again, the writers aren't trying to hide their political messaging. Quite the opposite, in fact.

The political messaging is the entire plot.

On Aug. 5, the day Season 4 premiered, "Ted Lasso" co-creator Brendan Hunt appeared on Sarah Spain's podcast. Spain is a radical left-wing activist who has referred to Vice President J.D. Vance as a "demon" and launched a disgusting personal smear of Sophie Cunningham for having the temerity to argue against "biological men" in women's sports.

Hunt chose Spain's show to help promote the new season, which felt like a very intentional promotional choice.

The following night, Jason Sudeikis, Hunt, Juno Temple and several members of the new cast appeared at an exclusive "Ted Lasso" event at the Paley Museum. Megan Rapinoe, another radical far-left-wing activist, served as the moderator.

The people behind "Ted Lasso" knew whose approval they wanted and went directly to Sarah Spain and Megan Rapinoe to seek it.

The interview with Hunt also made clear how central the women's team was to the show's return. He said Sudeikis kept thinking about doing the series with a women's team after Season 3. That idea led to a small writers' retreat intended to determine whether the show remained "fertile ground."

The writers decided it did.

In other words, women's soccer wasn't simply the setting selected after the decision to revive "Ted Lasso." It was the idea that convinced the creators to revive it.

Despite my reaction, plenty of people watched the Season 4 premiere.

According to Nielsen data provided by Apple, the episode generated 296.6 million viewing minutes in the United States across Aug. 4 and Aug. 5. More than 200 million minutes came on Aug. 5 alone, making "Ted Lasso" the most-streamed program in the country that day.

Apple called it the biggest launch in Apple TV history.

That's impressive, but it also isn't terribly surprising.

"Ted Lasso" was one of the most popular streaming shows in America during its original run. It won 13 Emmy Awards, became Apple's signature television series and disappeared for three years after what many viewers believed was its finale.

Of course people wanted to see it return.

Nielsen's first weekly report was also strong. "Ted Lasso" generated 866 million viewing minutes across 35 available episodes, including the first three seasons, during the week of Aug. 3 through Aug. 9. The Season 4 premiere accounted for 36% of that total, and the show ranked second among streaming originals.

But those figures establish only that people were interested in the return of "Ted Lasso." They don't tell us whether the audience stuck around as the season progressed.

OutKick/Fox News Digital reached out to Apple and asked for episode-by-episode viewing totals for the subsequent Season 4 episodes. We also asked whether the company had internal data showing how many viewers who started the premiere finished it and continued watching the season.

Apple did not respond.

The company eagerly supplied the figure that allowed it to announce the biggest premiere in the history of its streaming service. It became much less communicative when asked for the numbers that would show whether those viewers kept watching.

If the later episodes were setting similarly historic marks, it is reasonable to think Apple would be just as eager to publicize those numbers.

Instead, the company that celebrated the premiere hasn't released any viewing data on the show in over a month.

While that doesn't prove viewership collapsed after the premiere, there is no public evidence that the record-setting launch translated into equally historic retention.

TIME critic Judy Berman received the first four episodes of Season 4 for review. So, she saw Ted invoke his "white male privilege," Rebecca admit that she never considered a woman for the coaching job, Alice confront her over that decision, players struggle with pregnancy and childcare, sponsors abandon the women's team and wealthy investors get lectured about the patriarchy and their "fake allyship."

The show couldn't have worked harder to establish its progressive credentials.

Despite all of that, Berman's headline read: "Ted Lasso Doesn't Know What to Do With Women's Soccer."

Berman argued that Ted's presence could come across as "paternalistic" and said the character sometimes resembled a "cringey, try-hard male feminist." She complained that Rebecca and Keeley still felt filtered through the "male gaze" and noted that many qualified female coaches could have received Ted's job.

"A different coach is going to have to inspire those locker rooms, because Ted Lasso just doesn't belong," she concluded.

You know, for a group of people who constantly complain that men think women "don't belong" in sports, they sure don't seem to have a problem proclaiming that men don't belong in women's sports. Well, except the men who "identify" as women, of course. Those men are to be celebrated.

Variety critic Alison Herman wrote that "feminist commentary was never the series' strong suit" and argued that despite the show's pivot toward women, longtime male characters like Ted, Beard and Roy remain "load-bearing" and "space-occupying" protagonists.

The Times of London critic Carol Midgley criticized the decision to sideline Alice in favor of Ted and argued that other storylines played into gender stereotypes, concluding that "occasionally you could argue the show itself is sexist."

Apparently, building the season around women's sports, sexism, representation, unequal funding and male privilege wasn't enough.

Even one of the people enlisted to celebrate the season found another way the show elevated a man at women's expense.

At the end of Spain's interview with Hunt, she recounted a conversation in which Malala Yousafzai argued that the series should really be called "Rebecca." Her reasoning was that Ted's compassionate coaching style is possible only because Rebecca, as the club's owner, permits it. Spain said Malala believed a male owner would have fired Ted and hired a more traditionally masculine manager.

Spain later asked Sudeikis what he thought of Malala's argument.

"They're not changing the name," he replied, according to Spain.

Hunt was far more accommodating. Spain quoted him calling Malala "incredible" and saying, "Everything she says makes sense," before joking that Warner Bros. probably didn't want to relabel all the merchandise.

Think about the moving target here. "Ted Lasso" resurrected itself around a women's team, filled its opening episodes with feminist grievances, pushed its title character toward the sidelines and promoted the season alongside Sarah Spain and Megan Rapinoe.

The response was still that the woman wasn't receiving enough credit and perhaps the man's name should be removed from the title.

As of this writing, Season 4 holds an 88% critics score and a 69% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Based on those numbers, critics generally approved of the season's direction more than the audience did, yet prominent progressive reviewers still found new ideological shortcomings to condemn.

What was "Ted Lasso" supposed to do?

Hollywood studios repeatedly bend popular franchises around the demands of progressive critics. Writers center the "correct" political issues, diversify the cast, elevate female characters and turn familiar stories into vehicles for approved social messages.

The audience gets a less entertaining product and critics still aren't satisfied. So, what's the point?

You see, for the left-wing media, satisfaction would undermine the entire industry. A critic whose influence comes from identifying perceived sexism, racism, homophobia, transphobia and whatever other "isms" and "phobias" they will invent in the next few years has little incentive to declare that a mainstream television show handled everything correctly.

The standard changes because the criticism is the product.

Hollywood keeps playing along, presumably because executives want favorable coverage, awards and protection from the online backlash that comes with refusing to follow the approved script.

Yet "Ted Lasso" demonstrates how little that protection is worth.

The show's creators resurrected a beloved series and rebuilt it around the issues progressive television critics claim to care about most. They then took it directly to sympathetic figures in left-wing sports media for promotion.

The progressive critics still weren't happy.

At some point, Hollywood might consider making shows for the people watching them instead of people professionally committed to manufacturing grievances on behalf of whichever "marginalized group" the show has supposedly wronged.

item.title: Country music star pulled her Bible into bed with her to get through divorce
item.description: Karen Waldrup, a country music star based in Nashville, reveals how she channeled the heartbreak of her fall 2025 divorce into powerful new music, including "Keeping the Faith."
item.content:encoded:
Accustomed to performing under the bright lights of concert halls as well as TV studios during her time as a finalist on "The Voice," country music star Karen Waldrup of Nashville never anticipated the darkness and despair that would accompany a divorce.

But she told Fox News Digital this week in a moving interview how she got through the most "awful" times in the fall of 2025, even while recording new songs, including "Keeping the Faith" and "Just in Case," which is out Friday, Sept. 18.

The songs and the phrases have deep resonance with her Christian faith, she said. 

105 YEAR-OLD CREDITS THE GOOD LORD FOR HER LONG LIFE: ‘EVERY DAY IS A BLESSING’

"'Keeping the Faith' is one of my favorite songs I've ever been a part of," she said.

It's not just about "keeping the faith, it's about keeping the hope, keeping the dream, keeping the focus, keeping the optimism. I went through a really challenging time in the fall of 2025. ... It was awful. So many people know the disheartening horror of that experience, and it was terrible."

"But I decided to make a song, ‘Keeping the Faith,'" said the Louisiana-born singer-songwriter. 

"And the day that I tracked that song was a tough day. It was the toughest day that I've ever been in the studio. And I didn't know if it was even going to come out good because I felt so broken. 

‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT 

"But I think in the end, the song came out great because of the brokenness," she said. "I think you can kind of hear it in the vocal, the desperation of keeping the faith and saying, ‘Hey, you know what, no matter what goes on, you got to get back up and go, you got it. Pick it up. You got to keep the faith.’ And so I'm proud of that song."

Waldrup was not only a top 5 finalist on Season 25 of "The Voice," she’s a BMI songwriter and a member of the Recording Academy (NARAS) and the Country Music Association (CMA). She's won 12 Nashville Industry Music Awards and has seven studio albums and over 50 songs released worldwide. 

"After a lot of time, reflection and prayer, I’m ready to share that my marriage has ended in divorce," she wrote to fans in February on her Facebook page. "This has been a deeply personal journey, and I’ve taken the time I needed to process it privately. I’m grateful for the love, grace and support around me, and I appreciate kindness as I continue to move forward."

She told Fox News Digital, "There's a bridge [in the song ‘Keeping the Faith’] that says, 'There's a reason I'm still standing here stronger than I ever knew."

"And I think after you go through something like that, your whole dream of a lifelong marriage goes away and is no longer a part of your life — it's so heartbreaking. But after you come out of it, I truly believe that you are stronger. People are stronger from this experience."

"My faith definitely carried me through that season, the fall of 2025. I was very vulnerable," she said. 

"We were working on the record, and I had to keep going. I look at people like Dolly Parton or Reba [McEntire], and I think about how many times they had somebody pass away, and they had to get back up on stage — or they had their mom in the hospital or something, and they had to go play a show," she added. 

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"And when I was going through that, I was actually sleeping with my Bible every single night, in the bed with me at night. I was waking up every morning, opening my scripture and reading it. My faith was definitely the foundation of what got me through that."

She said her friends made a difference as well.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"My friends believed in me. They believed I would get through it. They never doubted me. And one of the things I did, I made a list of the top six people — one being God, so God plus five people — that I felt like I could really talk to about what I was going through without them making me feel worse."

"And I tried to really only talk to those five people," said Waldrup. "Sometimes when you're going through something like a divorce, everyone has their opinions. Everyone has all these different things that people want to say. And so I found that was a really helpful thing.

"When you're going through something tough in life, rather than listening to the opinions of 50 people, you can kind of go, OK, these are the five people that, when I talk to this person, make me feel like I'm gonna get through this. And those are the people that I really leaned on. So my faith, my scripture and my friends."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Waldrup said she believes she is "living God's purpose for my life."

"I do think part of my purpose in music is to inspire. I don't make my musical experience all about me," she said. "This music is a gift, this show is a gift, this moment is a gift."

And "I believe in giving," she added. 

"I don't really need to be important. All I need to do is do God's work. … He gave me this voice. And we're talking about faith, we're talking about music, we're talking about joy, we're talking about friendship, and about love — or the lack thereof. 

"There are so many things that we are called to talk about in life. And I do feel like I'm living God's purpose for my life."

Waldrup has performed in more than 15 countries. 

Her newest single "Just in Case" is available now.

item.title: Buffalo Bills fans pay eye-opening prices for beer and food at Highmark Stadium opener
item.description: Pinto Ron's bowling ball shots, beer horns and hour-long concession lines define the wild Bills Mafia tailgate scene in Orchard Park, New York.
item.content:encoded:
The sun is shining this morning in Buffalo, New York as I pump out an edition of Friday Screencaps before hopping in the car for the drive back around Lake Erie to a whole different world from what I just experienced in Orchard Park.

My mission going in from my boss was simple: Go ask questions, talk to the people and document the opening of the new Highmark Stadium. What I experienced was what I suspect it's like to be on a drug-induced trip like those people in San Francisco experience where they're taking dumps in the streets and hunched over in paralysis as the drugs run wild through the bloodstream.

Gameday in Buffalo is unlike anything I've ever experienced, and I've been to all the biggest mainstream sports experiences in the U.S.

NEWLY RELEASED DATA SHOWS WHICH AMERICAN CITIES HAVE THE MOST PASSIONATE FANBASES IN THE NFL

The locals don't even blink at the sight of guys like this who are about to delete 32 beers.

The real members of Bills Mafia have their own looks. Thousands of looks. They don't even blink at a 400-pounder walking around with his rack hanging out. This is a place where adults make the pilgrimage to the legendary Pinto Ron and Pizza Pete tailgate spot in the Hammer Lot where Pinto Ron's team of merry pranksters pour shots of liquor into a bowling ball finger hole.

Drinking the shot is just one part of the routine. Throwing the ball to the ground and then blowing on a vuvuzela is also included in the bit. For the ladies, Ron's crew provides cherries that are dangled over their faces. Most of the classy women will not suck the cherry off the stem. Some, however, go for the full experience.

I assume the cherries have been soaked in moonshine.

BUFFALO BILLS' LATEST EDITION TO THEIR NEW STADIUM IS PREDICTABLY (AND PAINFULLY) ON BRAND

Hundreds and hundreds of people drink the shot out of the same hole over the course of a tailgate. Sanitation isn't a thing here. The liquor kills the germs.

Pinto Ron's team also cooks right on the hood of the most famous Pinto in Buffalo. Bacon and dogs were on the menu Thursday. Yes, I'm told the Pinto runs.

LIONS AVOID FRANCHISE-WORST COLLAPSE AS DEFENSE STOPS SAINTS TWO-POINT CONVERSION IN OT

Meanwhile, about 20 yards from Ron's holy grail of tailgating, Lions fans had their own headquarters. That's where the infamous Tubgaters held court with their traveling hot tub that is mounted on a trailer. The owner tells me that when he rolls into town, he'll pull up to a house and ask the locals if he can fill up his tub. On Thursday, he had the water up to 98 degrees, but he assured me it could get up to 115 degrees for those really cold winter nights.

Buffalo Bills games are Disney World for NFL tailgating debauchery, but there's a method to the madness. People are cordial. Free food is very common. It's everywhere. Free liquor is everywhere. Friendship isn't hard to come by. You can arrive by yourself and leave with dozens of friends.

RYAN FITZPATRICK SAYS FRIENDS RAVING ABOUT HIGHMARK STADIUM DESPITE HARSH CRITICS: 'ABSOLUTELY UNBELIEVABLE'

Needless to say, I'll be back. My dad needs to see this.

item.title: The AI revolution could become a national security disaster if we aren't careful
item.description: America hosts 75% of global high-performance compute, but moratoriums on AI data centers risk ceding that strategic advantage to China and rivals.
item.content:encoded:
Reindustrialization is alive in America. Yet the recent backlash on artificial intelligence (AI) data centers reveals we have not learned from our offshoring mistakes: creating dependencies that will not be easily reversed.

Whether or not AI data centers are built in America, AI is here to stay. Either we choose to shape the trajectory of AI technology by embracing the AI data center buildout or cede this advantage to other nations that are eager to lead the AI race. China, for example, announced nearly $300 billion in data center investment through 2030, not including private sector spending. India is offering a 20-year tax holiday for foreign cloud operators and the Republic of Korea is offering regulatory relief. Meanwhile, many Americans are calling for moratoriums.

The national security consequences of who hosts AI data centers go beyond competition with China. If we do not build AI data centers in the United States, we risk everything that is inside the data centers: the data, compute and intellectual property (IP) that drive innovation, protect privacy and enable sovereignty. We will also forfeit our ability to set the security standards for this critical infrastructure.

LIZ PEEK: CHINA IS CHEERING AS THE LEFT BLOCKS AMERICA’S AI INFRASTRUCTURE

If AI data centers are the engines of AI innovation, data is the fuel. A significant amount of data is required to make AI useful, all of which must pass through AI data centers. Data, therefore, must be handled carefully — especially for privacy reasons — and viewed as a national asset.

Adversaries will view data routed through AI data centers as an opportunity to advance their own AI ambitions. Data may be collected for espionage purposes or to accelerate adversaries’ own AI models, as we have seen China do time and again in cyberspace and through adversarial distillation. Adversaries may also conduct adversarial attacks during model training, which could, without our knowledge, degrade and manipulate data that determines the performance of AI models. Either way, insecure or compromised data impacts everyone — from large businesses to individuals — and exposes potentially sensitive information. Then there is compute. America currently hosts 75% of global high-performance compute, making it a true strategic advantage.

CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN

Strong export controls on advanced compute enable us to widen America’s AI lead against adversaries and work with allies and partners to shape the trajectory of AI. Our commitment to increased domestic semiconductor production through implementation of the CHIPS and Science Act is reinforcing our lead with new U.S. capacity. But where do chips go once we have them? Many of them go to AI data centers.

By sending AI data centers overseas, the chips will follow — and potentially the businesses that supply them. Re-offshoring will have a detrimental impact on U.S. resiliency and the U.S. economy, which has prepared for the reindustrialization of semiconductor manufacturing for the past four years.

CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE

Today, China’s semiconductors are a few generations behind the leading-edge due to U.S. export controls on high-end chips and equipment. But if chips are increasingly housed overseas where we cannot enforce security standards, we may increase the ease of remote access instead of closing this loophole, further enabling China to accelerate its own AI development.

Relying on overseas AI data centers will also kneecap us in the event of a global crisis because other nations — not the United States — will decide where to surge compute. There is no guarantee that America will receive any of that capacity, but what we do receive will be slow because it will not be on our shores.

Compute capacity is already severely constrained and will only become more limited as demand grows for AI tools. This will impact our military, which already faces a potential compute bottleneck, and our innovators powering new breakthroughs, including researchers, students and startups. Having AI data centers in America ensures we can comfortably prioritize access during a crisis while continuing to foster our innovation economy and technical workforce.

Tying together data and compute is AI IP, which includes the AI models and model weights that have enabled America to stay at the frontier. IP is already a well-known target for the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and this extends to AI. China has already engaged in IP theft through adversarial distillation to compete with proprietary, American frontier models. Sending AI data centers overseas is like handing IP over to the CCP, which they will continue to use for their own market dominance and, presumably, their military advantage. Luckily, America currently hosts the most AI data centers. However, given about 60% of announced projects for this year have yet to begin construction, this lead cannot be taken for granted. As companies and policymakers seize this moment to reframe the narrative about resource use and benefit to local communities, three immediate actions can build public confidence and ensure America’s security interests.

CHINESE BOT FARM CAUGHT RED-HANDED TRYING TO INFLUENCE HEATED AI DATA CENTER DEBATE

First, America should leverage federal land to start rapid AI data center buildout. In July 2025, President Trump signed an Executive Order to open up federal land and streamline permitting for commercial AI data centers. By using this authority, America can ensure AI is viewed as a common good instead of a local burden. It also puts the responsibility on the U.S. government, rather than local communities, to work with data center developers to scale AI using modest resources.

Second, the Commerce Department should leverage the AI Exports Program to promote secure, global AI data center buildout with allies and partners. Allies and partners need AI capacity as much as the United States, and we should help enable their success. Standards for cyber and physical security of AI data centers are vital to securing and shaping AI use, but are still in development. The AI Exports Program, which aims to share the American tech stack with allies and partners, can be the enforcement mechanism to standardize safe and secure AI data center operations overseas. Through this program, we can mitigate the impact of insider threats and natural disasters; failures of interdependencies, such as water and energy; and compromise of data, compute and IP. By setting these expectations through an established program, companies can confidently build and other countries will know how to leverage the American tech stack for their own advantage, reinforcing it as the secure alternative to China’s tech stack.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Third, we must save room for AI data center improvements. Although we do not want to stall AI data center buildout, which erodes their value, it is worth asking if the pace of this buildout is necessary to stay ahead in AI. Not every data center proposed is expected to be built, but estimates project that we could reach $7 trillion in global AI data center investment by 2030. The domino effect of more compute is greater opportunity to innovate better methods to power AI that may not require a massive data center, or to improve AI models so that they do not need as much power. We must give innovators time to make these breakthroughs, and give us the flexibility to adapt.

America is poised to lead or lose the AI industrial revolution — a physical representation of its security interests. It must choose to lead by embracing AI data center buildout in the United States.

item.title: Ex-Dem insider reveals why Biden's daughter threatened to sue her: 'Bordered on parody'
item.description: Lindy Li reveals Ashley Biden threatened to sue her over claims about Joe Biden's cognitive decline, sharing screenshots of the since-deleted post.
item.content:encoded:
Ashley Biden, the daughter of former President Joe Biden and First Lady Jill Biden, threatened to sue a former Democratic fundraiser for spilling secret internal discussions about her father’s cognitive and political decline in the 2024 presidential election.

Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched her party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about Biden's decline in the 2024 election, said Ashley Biden posted the threat to Instagram in February of last year.

"They wanted to scare me. That was the goal," Li told Fox News Digital.

Li’s account of the threat, in her view, was one of the many attempts to intimidate her that she received after deciding to speak out about the fear, disorganization and secrecy that had paved the path for Biden to run for re-election in 2024 despite looming concerns about his age. Also, the fact that those threats never materialized is evidence to Li that even her critics recognize the validity of her testimony.

EX-DEM FUNDRAISER TORCHES BIDEN AS BOOK LAUNCH IMPLODES: 'NO ONE WANTS TO READ'

Li described the threat from Ashley Biden in her book, "Unburdened."

"Ashley later threatened to sue me for saying there was a cover-up of her father’s decline, lashing out on Instagram with a bravado so crude it bordered on parody: ‘This woman is a bonavide [sic] liar. Karma is a real bad b----, Lindy,’" she wrote.

"’I don’t know you but can’t wait to meet your a-- in court. Ready for a lawsuit? Let’s go! I won’t put up with this BS anymore.’"

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Li showed screenshots of the post, which she said was taken down just a day later.

She recalled thinking it was odd; beyond the lawsuit threat, Ashley Biden claimed she didn’t know who Li was. But Li had met Ashley Biden on a number of occasions and shared pictures of the two of them with Fox News Digital as proof.

"Doesn’t even pass the smell test," Li said.

EX-DEM INSIDER DROPS BOMBSHELL ON WHERE HARRIS RANKED IN SECRET POLL FOR BIDEN REPLACEMENTS

As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris, Li worked closely with top donors, high-profile members of the party and the Democratic National Committee (DNC). When she decided to go public with revelations about Biden’s age, she said the retaliation began immediately.

"When I went on Shannon’s show to say Biden needs to step aside — and three hours later he did — my access immediately vanished and all my fears about speaking up were justified," Li told Fox News Digital.

"I knew that if I spoke up my life would be ruined and frankly, in that respect, it was. I was never invited to the White House again, never spoke to Biden again. Prior to that, I was invited to the White House every two to three weeks. There was always some event."

When Li brought Ashley Biden’s threat to her legal representation, her lawyers dismissed the possibility but said that the Bidens would likely try to avoid a painful disclosure battle that could drag more details into the public eye over his cognitive decline.

EX-DEM INSIDER EXPOSES WHAT HARRIS TOLD TOP DONORS DAYS BEFORE BIDEN DROPPED OUT: 'INSULTING'

"My lawyer’s eyes lit up: ‘You want her to use you. The discovery would be incredible,’" she recalled. "Truth, after all, remains the strongest shield against defamation."

"Everything I said was true so... I’m still waiting to hear exactly what I said that is legally actionable," Li said.

Representation for Ashley Biden did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Can tech really get you off your phone and into real life?
item.description: NewTree Social founder Maddy O'Connor built a community events app to help people discover local gatherings, wellness events and run clubs nearby.
item.content:encoded:
How many times have you picked up your phone to check one thing and found yourself still scrolling 30 minutes later? I know I've done it.

Our phones make it incredibly easy to stay connected. Yet something interesting seems to be happening at the same time. Many people are looking for more reasons to put those phones down and spend time with other people in the real world.

Run clubs are growing. Local gatherings are drawing attention. Phone-free events are popping up. People seem hungry for experiences that feel a little less like another feed.

That raises an interesting question: Could the same technology that keeps pulling us online also help get us back into real life? That idea is behind NewTree Social, an early-stage community events app from 29-year-old founder Maddy O'Connor. She wants people to use their phones to discover something happening nearby, make a plan and then go experience it. And the timing may be right.

RESTAURANTS BAN DINERS' PHONES DURING MEALS AS NO-SCROLL TREND GROWS: PUT IT AWAY OR ELSE

NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com.

There is some real data behind this shift. Eventbrite's 2026 Social Study surveyed people ages 18 to 35 in the U.S. and U.K. It found that 79% planned to attend more events in 2026. Among Gen Z respondents, 46% said they were limiting screen time and 74% said in-person experiences were more important than digital ones.

Now, keep in mind that this research comes from Eventbrite, a company whose business revolves around live events. Still, those numbers line up with something we are seeing play out in the real world.

Eventbrite says phone-free experiences listed on its platform grew 567% globally between 2024 and 2025. Attendance at those events rose 121%. The company based those numbers on events that used "phone-free" terminology in their title or description.

For people who have spent years with a smartphone within arm's reach, intentionally putting it away feels significant. It also creates an unusual opening for technology. Instead of asking how an app can keep you scrolling longer, what if the goal becomes helping you find something worth closing the app for?

That is where O'Connor comes in. She told CyberGuy that the idea for NewTree grew partly from her own experience living in Washington, D.C., without an established group of friends. Her experience changed depending on where she lived and whether she could find places where meeting new people felt natural.

At the same time, she was watching interest grow around run clubs, wellness events, social clubs and other in-person experiences. So she started building around that behavior.

NewTree is designed to help people discover local activities and meet others through something they already want to do. I think that part is important.

Walking into a room of strangers solely because you are supposed to meet people can feel awkward. Walking into a fitness class, community event or gathering you already find interesting gives you a reason to be there before you ever introduce yourself. For someone who recently moved or simply wants to expand a social circle, that could make taking the first step a little easier.

Open NewTree and the basic experience should feel familiar. There is a feed. You browse events nearby. You can RSVP and get reminders about something you want to attend.

But the idea behind that feed is a little different. O'Connor comes from a graphic design background and told CyberGuy that she deliberately wanted NewTree to feel more like a social platform than a traditional events directory.

The app currently focuses on community, fitness and wellness events around Tampa, St. Pete and Clearwater. Apple describes it as an app for discovering local events, RSVPing and meeting new people.

Hosts can add photos and videos to event listings. Users can browse what is happening around them and RSVP from their phones. O'Connor also wants reviews to play a bigger role in what people discover. She says reviews of a host's events can affect how those events perform in the feed instead of simply sitting on a profile.

There is something almost funny about the concept. You open another social-style app because you want to spend less of your social life inside apps. But maybe that is exactly the point.

EXPERTS REVEAL WHY 'NONNAMAXXING' TREND MAY IMPROVE MENTAL, PHYSICAL HEALTH

NewTree is entering a crowded space. Meetup, Eventbrite and Facebook already help people discover events nearby, and both Meetup and Eventbrite offer personalized recommendations.

So what is NewTree trying to do differently? O'Connor says she wants the experience to feel more like a social platform built specifically around getting people together in person. She also says reviews can influence how a host's events perform in the feed, so better-reviewed experiences can potentially receive greater visibility. During NewTree's early pilot, O'Connor is personally reviewing and approving hosts before their events can appear publicly.

None of those ideas completely reinvents event discovery. The bet is that putting them together in a more curated, community-focused experience will give people another useful way to find things to do and meet people nearby. Whether that gives people enough reason to add NewTree to the apps they already use is one of the biggest things the company still has to prove.

Here is what I would be watching. Does NewTree help people make plans they actually follow through on? Getting someone to download an app is one thing. Getting them to put on shoes, leave home and show up somewhere is much harder.

The idea works if you spend a few minutes browsing NewTree, find something interesting and eventually put the phone back in your pocket because you have somewhere to go.

It becomes a lot less interesting if people simply scroll through another feed filled with things they might someday do. O'Connor is very open about just how early NewTree is.

She told CyberGuy that NewTree is pre-traction and pre-revenue. Tampa Bay is the starting point because she wants to prove that people will use the platform in one market before trying to expand throughout Florida and eventually nationwide. So there is a long way to go. But the behavior NewTree is betting on already appears to be taking shape.

Of course, using an app to find events where you may meet strangers brings some very real safety questions. O'Connor says she has taken a hands-on approach during NewTree's MVP stage. She told CyberGuy that she personally reviews and approves hosts before their events can appear on the platform. Users can report content or other users and block people. Hosts can also remove or report attendees.

NewTree's current support page says business profiles are reviewed before they can post. However, there is an important limitation. A verified badge means NewTree says it has confirmed that the business is who it claims to be. It does not mean NewTree is endorsing or guaranteeing a specific event.

NewTree's terms go further. They say events are generally operated independently by outside hosts and that NewTree does not ordinarily perform criminal background checks or identity verification on users, attendees, hosts or organizers.

So I would still do some homework before showing up at an unfamiliar event. Look up the organizer independently. Check the venue. If you are uncomfortable going alone, bring someone you trust. Technology can help you find people. It cannot remove all of the risks that come with meeting people you do not know.

Privacy deserves a close look too. O'Connor told CyberGuy that NewTree collects basic account information, including your name, email, date of birth and location. She says the app can use a saved profile location or, with your permission, your device location.

She also said the information is stored through NewTree's Supabase database, with database-level access controls designed to limit who can access different information. When someone RSVPs to a free event, O'Connor says the host receives the attendee's name, email and location information so they can manage and communicate with attendees.

1 IN 6 ADULTS PLAGUED BY LONELINESS AS RESEARCHERS REVEAL LASTING IMPACT OF COVID PANDEMIC

Another detail could cause some confusion. Apple currently gives NewTree a 13+ age rating. NewTree itself says you must be at least 18 years old to create an account or use the platform.

O'Connor told CyberGuy that Apple's 13+ label reflects its content-based App Store rating rather than the minimum age NewTree allows on the platform. So, despite what you may see on the App Store listing, NewTree says the service itself is for adults 18 and older.

Right now, Apple lists NewTree as an iPhone app. O'Connor told CyberGuy that Android support is planned but not available yet.

The business model is still taking shape too. O'Connor says she is leaning toward keeping the app free for users while eventually offering optional premium tools for businesses and hosts. Exactly what those paid features would include has not been decided.

So I would look at NewTree for what it is today: a very early app built around a much larger change in the way some people are thinking about technology.

Most of us could probably use a few more reasons to put the phone down and do something in the real world. Our phones have become where we communicate, work, watch videos and fill just about every empty moment.

Sometimes the screen starts taking the place of the experiences it was supposed to help us find. Maybe the better approach is expecting more from the technology we already use.

If an app helps you discover a local event, try something you would never have considered or meet someone you otherwise never would have crossed paths with, the phone becomes the starting point. Then it can get out of the way.

I like that idea. Use the technology to find something worth doing. Then look up from the screen and go do it.

What stands out to me here is how good technology has become at keeping us looking down. Notifications pull us back in. Feeds always have something else waiting. Before you know it, another chunk of your day has disappeared into a screen. Now we are seeing signs that many people want something different. They still want technology, but they also want more opportunities to be around people in the real world. NewTree has a lot to prove. But I like the problem O'Connor is trying to solve. Your phone already knows how to keep you home and entertained for hours. Maybe the next really useful social app will be the one that gives you a good reason to leave.

Would you use an app designed to get you off your phone and out meeting people, or does downloading another social app defeat the whole purpose? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.
